backTranslations.41: Before the visit: Add the visit date in the Visit tab. MenoMap will show how ready your notes are and what could strengthen them. Choose the topics and questions most important to you; limit yourself to three or four. Create notes from the last 30 or 90 days. Check that your medication list is up to date. At the visit: Hand over or show the first page. It is designed to be readable in under a minute: numbers, averages, a heat calendar and your questions. Start with the question most important to you. If your doctor speaks another language, you can create the notes in that language. What the notes are and are not: It is a summary of what you entered and of what you chose to bring over from the Health app. They are not a diagnosis or a full medical record, and any patterns they contain are a coincidence check, not proof of cause. The doctor may ask questions the notes do not answer, and that is normal. After the visit: Add each new medication with a start date. In a few weeks MenoMap can show your entries from before starting the medication and after it, which makes the next assessment easier.
backTranslations.42: Menopause is a single moment in time: the day when 12 consecutive months without a period have passed, if nothing else explains it (e.g. pregnancy, certain medications or surgery). In many countries it happens on average just after fifty, but often occurs at any point between roughly age 45 and 55. Perimenopause is the period of several years leading up to that moment. Hormone levels rise and fall unevenly, so periods can become irregular, heavier, lighter, more frequent or less frequent. Many changes associated with menopause, such as hot flashes, night sweats, changes in sleep and mood, often begin precisely when periods are still occurring. Perimenopause can last a few years or much longer and goes differently for each person. Postmenopause is all the time after those 12 months have passed. Some symptoms fade over time, others can persist for years. Menopause can also happen earlier because of surgery removing the ovaries, some cancer treatments or other illnesses. Menopause before age 40 is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency and is worth discussing with a doctor. How it is recognised: In many people over 45, a doctor recognises perimenopause or menopause based on your history and symptoms. Blood tests are not always needed, because hormone levels change from day to day. They are more often ordered when someone is younger or the picture is unclear. What MenoMap does and does not do: MenoMap cannot tell you what stage you are at. It can, however, reliably record what you notice: flashes, sleep, mood and treatment, so that you and your doctor can look at the same picture.

backTranslations.162: Doctors call hot flashes and night sweats vasomotor symptoms. A hot flash is a sudden feeling of heat, often on the face, neck and chest, sometimes with redness, sweating, a fast heartbeat or chills afterward. Night sweats are the same during sleep and can be strong enough to wake you or soak the bedding. They are among the most common changes in menopause. Some people have a few and they are mild; others have many a day and they disrupt work and sleep. In some people they subside within a few years, in others they persist much longer. What may favour them: Many people notice a link with alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, hot rooms, stress or heavy bedding. It looks very different in different people, so tracking your own tags may be more useful than a general list. There are also other causes: Redness and sweating can also result from thyroid problems, infections, some medications, anxiety and other illnesses. If your symptoms do not fit the typical picture, or are accompanied by weight loss, fever or feeling unwell, tell your doctor. How to describe them well: Useful information for a visit: how many there are in a day and night, roughly; how strong they are and how long they last; what they interrupt: sleep, work, conversation, exercise; what seems to precede them; what you have already tried and whether it changed anything. MenoMap's flash button and after-the-fact logging exist to capture exactly this information without much effort. Help is available: There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatments and practical ways of coping. Which of them suit you is a topic for a conversation with your doctor.

backTranslations.278: Heart sensations have many causes. If they are new, severe, or accompanied by chest pain, shortness of breath or fainting, seek medical help immediately.
backTranslations.291: Hormone therapy (often called hormone replacement therapy, HRT, or MHT) replaces some of the estrogen that the body produces less of during menopause. The leading guidelines describe it as an effective treatment for hot flashes and night sweats in many people; it may also help with other symptoms. It comes in different forms: patches, gels, sprays, tablets, and low-dose vaginal preparations for local symptoms such as dryness. People who still have a uterus are usually prescribed a progestogen together with estrogen, to protect the lining of the uterus. Benefits and risks depend on the person: on age, time since periods stopped, personal and family history (e.g. breast cancer, clots, stroke or heart disease) and on the type and route of treatment. That is why it is a decision to make with a doctor who knows your history, not something an app can decide. Questions that often come up: Is hormone therapy one of the options for me, and why or why not? What type and form of treatment would be appropriate in my case and why? What benefits can I expect and how quickly? What is my personal risk and how does it compare with no treatment? What should I watch for and when should we reassess? If you already use it, record it in MenoMap (You -> Medications). MenoMap will show your flashes before starting and after - as a coincidence check, not proof - so that you have something concrete to discuss at the check-up. MenoMap never suggests starting, stopping or changing a medication.
backTranslations.292: Hormone therapy is a decision to make with a doctor
backTranslations.293: Hormone therapy is not right for everyone, and some people simply prefer other solutions. There are several. Prescription medicines: There is evidence that some non-hormonal medicines reduce hot flashes. They include certain medicines originally developed to treat other conditions and a newer group of medicines designed specifically for hot flashes. Each has its own benefits, side effects and interactions, so a doctor can help you weigh them. Talking and mind-body approaches: There is evidence that cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) adapted to menopause makes hot flashes and night sweats less burdensome, and improves sleep. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied. Practical changes many people find helpful: layers of clothing that can be taken off quickly; a fan at the desk and at the bed; a cooler bedroom and breathable bedding; noticing and limiting your own triggers (MenoMap's tags and experiments help with this); regular activity and a steady sleep rhythm. Supplements and herbal preparations: For many of them the evidence is mixed or limited, quality varies, and some interact with other medicines. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about everything you take, including products without a prescription. Make one change at a time: MenoMap's two-week experiments compare your own entries from before the change and during it, and that is easier to judge than a feeling alone.

backTranslations.403: MenoMap is a wellbeing-tracking app and an educational tool. It does not diagnose menopause or any other condition, does not prescribe or change treatment, and does not replace the care of a qualified doctor. If your symptoms worry you, or if you have bleeding after menopause, chest pain, a sudden severe headache, weakness on one side of the body, difficulty breathing or fainting, use an in-person doctor's visit or emergency help.
backTranslations.416: Most visits are short, and it is hard to recall a whole month of nights on the spot. Usually one remembers the last days or the worst ones. A simple record fills that gap. What a diary gives the doctor: how often symptoms occur and how strong they are, not just that they occur; whether it is better, worse or unchanged; what was going on around them: sleep, alcohol, stress, medications; a starting point for comparison if you try some treatment. Keep it simple: A diary helps only if you keep it. MenoMap relies on a flash button that works with one tap and an evening summary with four questions, so it takes seconds, not a whole notebook. Two weeks is a good start: Entries from two to four weeks usually give a clearer picture than one bad week. Bring your questions too: Write down what matters most to you: the symptom that bothers you most, what you want to try or avoid, and anything that worries you. The Visit tab in MenoMap helps choose questions and prints them together with the notes.

backTranslations.479: Once 12 months without a period have passed, any vaginal bleeding should be checked by a doctor, even if it occurred only once and even if it was only spotting or a light pink or brown discharge. In most cases the cause turns out to be harmless. For example, thinning of the lining of the vagina or uterus is common. However, bleeding after menopause can sometimes be an early sign of a condition that is much easier to treat when detected early. That is why public health recommendations say to have it checked rather than wait. If you use hormone therapy, some kinds of bleeding may be expected, depending on the type of treatment. Bleeding that is unexpected with your treatment, heavier than usual or occurs at the wrong time should also be checked. What to do: Contact a doctor or healthcare facility and say that you have had bleeding after menopause. Write down the date, amount and anything else you noticed. MenoMap can store this for you (You -> Cycle). MenoMap cannot tell you why the bleeding occurred. It will remind you to have it checked and will include it in the visit notes.

backTranslations.529: Poor sleep is one of the most common complaints in midlife and rarely has a single cause. Night sweats can wake you directly, or make you too hot or too sweaty to fall asleep again. Other common factors: needing to urinate at night; anxiety or racing thoughts; alcohol, which can help you fall asleep but usually fragments sleep in the second half of the night; caffeine later in the day; pain, restless legs or a partner's snoring; snoring or pauses in breathing, which can be a sign of sleep apnoea (worth mentioning, especially if you are very sleepy during the day). What usually helps: a cool, dark room; breathable bedding and layers of clothing that can be taken off; a steady wake-up time; less alcohol before bed. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured, well-studied method and many doctors can direct you to it. What to record: For a week or two note your sleep rating, night flashes, alcohol and late caffeine. MenoMap's evening summary and flash log let you do this in a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can show your sleep and wrist temperature from the Health app next to night sweats - as context, not as an explanation. When to get checked: Talk to a doctor if poor sleep affects your safety (e.g. while driving), mood or daily life, or if you notice pauses in breathing or gasping at night.
